title: UNIT 1: RELATIONS AND FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Relation → a set of ordered pairs that describes a relationship between elements of two sets.

✓ Function → a special type of relation in which every first component is related to exactly one second component.

title: 1.1 RELATIONS
notes:
✓ Relation → a set of ordered pairs used to describe a relationship between elements.

An ordered pair is written as (x, y).

◆ x → first component or first coordinate.
◆ y → second component or second coordinate.

Two ordered pairs are equal only when their corresponding components are equal:
(a, b) = (c, d) ⇔ a = c and b = d.

Example:
(2, 5) ≠ (5, 2), because the order of the components is different.

→ Any set of ordered pairs is a relation.

title: RELATION FROM A TO B
notes:
✓ Given sets A and B, a relation R from A to B is a set of ordered pairs (x, y), where x ∈ A and y ∈ B.

R ⊆ A × B.

◆ A × B → Cartesian product of A and B, containing all possible ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B.

Example:
If A = {1, 2} and B = {a, b}, then:
A × B = {(1,a), (1,b), (2,a), (2,b)}.

→ A relation from A to B can contain any subset of these ordered pairs.

title: DOMAIN AND RANGE OF A RELATION
notes:
✓ Domain of R → the set of all first components of the ordered pairs in R.

Dom(R) = {x ∈ A | (x,y) ∈ R for some y ∈ B}.

✓ Range of R → the set of all second components of the ordered pairs in R.

Ran(R) = {y ∈ B | (x,y) ∈ R for some x ∈ A}.

Example:
R = {(45,65), (48,68), (41,62), (46,66), (50,70)}

Domain = {41,45,46,48,50}
Range = {62,65,66,68,70}.

→ Domain → collect the first coordinates.
→ Range → collect the second coordinates.

title: REPRESENTATIONS OF RELATIONS
notes:
A relation can be represented in several ways:

◆ As a set of ordered pairs.
◆ Using a table of values.
◆ Using a mapping/arrow diagram.
◆ Using a graph in the coordinate plane.
◆ Using an equation or rule involving x and y.

Example:
R = {(1,2), (2,4), (3,6)}

Table → pairs the x-values with their corresponding y-values.

Mapping → 1 → 2, 2 → 4, 3 → 6.

Equation → y = 2x.

Graph → plot (1,2), (2,4) and (3,6) on the coordinate plane.

title: RELATIONS DEFINED BY EQUATIONS
notes:
A relation may be defined by an equation involving x and y.

Example:
R = {(x,y) : y = 2x − 1, x,y ∈ ℝ}.

For x = 0:
y = 2(0) − 1 = −1 → (0,−1).

For x = 2:
y = 2(2) − 1 = 3 → (2,3).

◆ The domain consists of the allowed x-values.
◆ The range consists of the corresponding y-values.

When a relation is represented graphically, its domain corresponds to x-values appearing on the graph and its range corresponds to y-values appearing on the graph.

title: 1.2 INVERSES OF RELATIONS
notes:
✓ Inverse relation → a relation obtained by interchanging the first and second components of every ordered pair.

If:
R = {(x,y), ...}

then:
R⁻¹ = {(y,x), ...}.

Example:
R = {(1,2), (3,4), (5,6)}

Therefore:
R⁻¹ = {(2,1), (4,3), (6,5)}.

Important properties:
Dom(R⁻¹) = Ran(R)
Ran(R⁻¹) = Dom(R).

title: FINDING THE INVERSE FROM AN EQUATION
notes:
To find the inverse relation of an equation:

1. Interchange x and y.
2. Rearrange the resulting equation if necessary.
3. Write the inverse relation.

Example:
Given:
y = 2x − 5

Interchange x and y:
x = 2y − 5

Solve for y:
2y = x + 5

Therefore:
y = (x + 5)/2.

→ The inverse relation is obtained by reversing the roles of x and y.

title: GRAPH OF AN INVERSE RELATION
notes:
✓ The graph of an inverse relation is obtained by reflecting the graph of the original relation in the line:

y = x

Example:
If (2,5) lies on the graph of R, then (5,2) lies on the graph of R⁻¹.

The points (2,5) and (5,2) are reflections of each other across y = x.

→ Therefore, the graph of R⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of R about the line y = x.

title: 1.3 TYPES OF FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Function → a relation in which each element of the set of first components is related to exactly one element of the set of second components.

Example of a function:
R = {(−1,0), (0,−3), (2,−3), (3,0), (4,5)}.

Each first component appears only once with one second component.

Not a function:
R = {(6,1), (7,3), (0,2), (6,4)}.

→ The first component 6 is related to both 1 and 4.

✓ A function cannot assign two different outputs to the same input.

title: FUNCTION NOTATION
notes:
If f is a function from A to B, it can be written as:

f : A → B

◆ Dom(f) = A.
◆ Ran(f) is a subset of B.

If y = f(x), then f(x) is read as “f of x.”

Example:
If f(x) = 2x + 3:

f(1) = 2(1) + 3 = 5.

f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11.

→ x is the input and f(x) is the corresponding output.

title: VERTICAL LINE TEST
notes:
✓ Vertical Line Test → a graphical test used to determine whether a relation represents a function.

A set of points in the coordinate plane represents a function if and only if no vertical line intersects the graph at more than one point.

Example:
A parabola y = x² passes the vertical line test because every x-value gives exactly one y-value.

A circle such as x² + y² = 4 fails the test because some vertical lines intersect it at two points.

→ One x-value → exactly one y-value.

title: 1.3.1 POWER FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Power function → a function of the form:

f(x) = axʳ

where a is a nonzero real number and r is a real number.

Examples of power functions:
f(x) = 3x²
f(x) = 5x³
f(x) = x⁴/³
f(x) = −4x⁻³.

◆ Exponential functions such as 2ˣ are not power functions.
◆ Logarithmic functions such as log₃x are not power functions.

→ The variable must occur as the base and have a constant exponent.

title: POWER FUNCTIONS: EVEN POSITIVE POWERS
notes:
For functions of the form:
f(x) = xⁿ
where n is a positive even integer:

◆ Domain = ℝ.
◆ Range = [0,∞).
◆ The graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
◆ f(x) ≥ 0 for every real x.

Examples:
f(x) = x²
f(x) = x⁴.

For x²:
(−2)² = 4, (−1)² = 1, 0² = 0, 1² = 1, 2² = 4.

→ Increasing distance from the origin in either direction produces larger positive y-values.

title: POWER FUNCTIONS: ODD POSITIVE POWERS
notes:
For functions of the form:
f(x) = xⁿ
where n is a positive odd integer:

◆ Domain = ℝ.
◆ Range = ℝ.
◆ The graph passes through the origin.
◆ The graph has the characteristic odd-power shape.

Examples:
f(x) = x³
f(x) = x⁵.

For f(x) = x³:
(−2)³ = −8
(−1)³ = −1
0³ = 0
1³ = 1
2³ = 8.

→ Negative x-values produce negative y-values.

title: POWER FUNCTIONS WITH FRACTIONAL POWERS
notes:
✓ Power functions with positive fractional exponents can have restricted domains depending on the denominator of the exponent.

Examples:
f(x) = x¹/² = √x
f(x) = x¹/⁴ = ⁴√x.

For these functions:
◆ Domain = [0,∞).
◆ Range = [0,∞).

For an odd root, such as:
f(x) = x¹/³ = ³√x

◆ Domain = ℝ.
◆ Range = ℝ.

→ The parity of the root denominator determines whether negative x-values are allowed.

title: POWER FUNCTIONS WITH NEGATIVE POWERS
notes:
✓ Negative powers produce reciprocal-type functions.

Example:
f(x) = x⁻¹ = 1/x.

x = 0 is not allowed.
Domain = ℝ \ {0}.
Range = ℝ \ {0}.

For:
f(x) = x⁻² = 1/x²

Domain = ℝ \ {0}.
Range = (0,∞).

→ Negative powers generally produce graphs with x = 0 excluded from the domain and often have vertical behavior near x = 0.

title: 1.3.2 MODULUS (ABSOLUTE VALUE) FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Absolute value of a real number x → its distance from 0 on the number line.

|x| = x, when x ≥ 0.
|x| = −x, when x < 0.

Examples:
|5| = 5
|0| = 0
|−5| = 5.

→ Absolute value is always non-negative:
|x| ≥ 0.

The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero.

title: PROPERTIES OF ABSOLUTE VALUE
notes:
Important properties:

|x| ≥ 0.

|x| = 0 ⇔ x = 0.

|−x| = |x|.

|xy| = |x||y|.

|x/y| = |x|/|y|, y ≠ 0.

|x|² = x².

Example:
|−3 × 4| = |−12| = 12.

Also:
|−3||4| = 3 × 4 = 12.

→ Absolute value removes the sign while preserving magnitude.

title: MODULUS FUNCTION AND ITS GRAPH
notes:
✓ The modulus function is:

f(x) = |x|.

It can be written as:

f(x) = x, for x ≥ 0
f(x) = −x, for x < 0.

◆ Domain = ℝ.
◆ Range = [0,∞).
◆ Graph → V-shaped curve with vertex at (0,0).
◆ The graph is symmetric about the y-axis.

Example:
f(x) = |x − 1|

→ The vertex is at (1,0), and the graph opens upward.

title: TRANSFORMATIONS OF MODULUS FUNCTIONS
notes:
Modulus functions can be shifted and stretched.

Examples:
f(x) = |x| → vertex (0,0).

f(x) = |x| − 1 → vertex (0,−1).

f(x) = |x − 2| → vertex (2,0).

f(x) = 2|x| → vertical stretch by factor 2.

General form:
f(x) = a|x − h| + k

→ Vertex = (h,k).

◆ a > 0 → opens upward.
◆ a < 0 → opens downward.

title: 1.3.3 SIGNUM FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Signum function → a piecewise function that indicates the sign of a real number.

It is denoted by sgn x.

sgn x = 1, for x > 0
sgn x = 0, for x = 0
sgn x = −1, for x < 0.

Examples:
sgn(5) = 1
sgn(0) = 0
sgn(−7) = −1.

◆ Domain = ℝ.
◆ Range = {−1, 0, 1}.

title: SIGNUM FUNCTION AND ABSOLUTE VALUE
notes:
For x ≠ 0:

sgn x = |x|/x.

Equivalently:

sgn x = x/|x|, for x ≠ 0.

Example:
For x = −4:
sgn(−4) = |−4|/(−4) = 4/(−4) = −1.

For x = 6:
sgn(6) = 6/|6| = 6/6 = 1.

→ At x = 0, sgn(0) = 0.

title: 1.3.4 GREATEST INTEGER (FLOOR OR STEP) FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Greatest Integer Function → the function whose value is the greatest integer less than or equal to x.

It is denoted by:
f(x) = [x]

Examples:
[10.7] = 10
[−12.4] = −13
[−18] = −18.

→ For negative numbers, remember that the answer must be the integer immediately below or equal to the number.

Example:
[−1.9] = −2, not −1.

title: GRAPH OF THE GREATEST INTEGER FUNCTION
notes:
For f(x) = [x]:

◆ Domain = ℝ.
◆ Range = the set of all integers.

For every integer n:
n ≤ x < n + 1 ⇒ [x] = n.

Examples:
0 ≤ x < 1 ⇒ [x] = 0.
1 ≤ x < 2 ⇒ [x] = 1.
−1 ≤ x < 0 ⇒ [x] = −1.

→ The graph has a step-like shape.
Each step includes its left endpoint and excludes its right endpoint.

title: GREATEST INTEGER EQUATIONS
notes:
✓ Greatest integer equations can be solved by using the definition:

[x] = n ⇔ n ≤ x < n + 1, where n is an integer.

Example:
Solve [x] = 3.

Using the definition:
3 ≤ x < 4.

Therefore:
x ∈ [3,4).

Example:
Solve [2 + [x]] = 5.

Let [x] = z.
Then:
[2 + z] = 5 → 5 ≤ 2 + z < 6.

Therefore:
3 ≤ z < 4.
Since z is an integer:
z = 3.
Thus [x] = 3, so:
3 ≤ x < 4.

title: 1.4 COMPOSITION OF FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Composition of functions → a new function obtained by using one function as the input of another function.

If f and g are functions, then:

(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)).

This means:
1. Apply f first.
2. Apply g to the result.

Example:
Let f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = x².

(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))
= g(x + 3)
= (x + 3)².

→ The order of composition is important.

title: COMPOSITION: f ∘ g
notes:
The composition:

(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).

Using:
f(x) = x + 3
g(x) = x²

we get:
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(x²)
= x² + 3.

Therefore:
(g ∘ f)(x) = (x + 3)²

while:
(f ∘ g)(x) = x² + 3.

→ In general:
f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ f.

Composition is generally not commutative.

title: DOMAIN OF A COMPOSITION
notes:
For:
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))

x must first belong to the domain of f, and f(x) must then belong to the domain of g.

✓ Therefore, the domain of a composition depends on both functions.

Example:
f(x) = √x
g(x) = 2x − 5.

For (g ∘ f)(x):
g(f(x)) = 2√x − 5.

Since √x is defined only for x ≥ 0:
Domain = [0,∞).

→ Always check the restrictions introduced by the inner function and the outer function.

title: IDENTITY FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Identity function → a function from a set A to itself defined by:

I(x) = x.

It is denoted by I.

Example:
If A = {1,2,3,4}, then:
I = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4)}.

For any function f:

I ∘ f = f.
f ∘ I = f.

Example:
If f(x) = 2x − 3:
(I ∘ f)(x) = I(2x − 3) = 2x − 3 = f(x).

title: 1.5 INVERSE FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Inverse function → the inverse relation of a function that is itself a function.

If the inverse of f is also a function, f is called invertible.

The inverse of f is denoted by:
f⁻¹.

Important:
Not every function has an inverse that is a function.

→ For an inverse function to exist as a function, the original function must give a unique output for each input and its inverse must also give a unique output for each input.

title: HOW TO FIND AN INVERSE FUNCTION
notes:
Given:
y = f(x)

To find f⁻¹:

1. Interchange x and y.
2. Solve for y in terms of x, if possible.
3. Write the result as:
y = f⁻¹(x).

Example:
f(x) = 3x + 2.

Start:
y = 3x + 2.

Interchange x and y:
x = 3y + 2.

Solve:
y = (x − 2)/3.

Therefore:
f⁻¹(x) = (x − 2)/3.

title: WHEN THE INVERSE IS NOT A FUNCTION
notes:
✓ The inverse of a function may fail to be a function.

Example:
f(x) = x³ − x + 1.

If two different x-values give the same output, then the inverse relation contains two different second components for the same first component.

For example:
f(−1) = 1
f(1) = 1.

Therefore, the inverse contains:
(1,−1) and (1,1).

→ Since 1 has two possible outputs in the inverse relation, the inverse is not a function.

A function must have an inverse relation that also satisfies the function condition.

title: IDENTITY AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ If f is invertible, then composing f with its inverse gives the identity function.

f⁻¹ ∘ f = I

and:
f ∘ f⁻¹ = I.

Example:
If f maps A to B and f⁻¹ maps B back to A, then:

f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Also:
f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

→ An inverse function reverses the action of the original function.

title: GRAPH OF AN INVERSE FUNCTION
notes:
✓ The graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the graph of the original function in the line:

y = x.

If (a,b) is on the graph of f, then (b,a) is on the graph of f⁻¹.

Example:
If f(2) = 5, then:
f⁻¹(5) = 2.

The graph contains the reflected points:
(2,5) ↔ (5,2).

→ The domain and range are interchanged:
Dom(f⁻¹) = Ran(f)
Ran(f⁻¹) = Dom(f).

title: UNIT 1 KEY TERMS & FORMULAS
notes:
◆ Relation → a set of ordered pairs.

◆ Ordered pair → (x,y), where x is the first component and y is the second component.

◆ Cartesian product → A × B, the set of all possible ordered pairs from A and B.

◆ Domain → set of first components.

◆ Range → set of second components.

◆ Inverse relation → obtained by interchanging x and y in every ordered pair.

Dom(R⁻¹) = Ran(R).

Ran(R⁻¹) = Dom(R).

◆ Function → every first component is related to exactly one second component.

◆ Vertical Line Test → no vertical line may intersect a function's graph more than once.

◆ Power function → f(x) = axʳ.

◆ Absolute value → |x| = x for x ≥ 0 and |x| = −x for x < 0.

◆ Modulus function → f(x) = |x|.

◆ Signum function → sgn x = 1 for x > 0, 0 for x = 0, −1 for x < 0.

◆ Greatest integer function → [x] is the greatest integer ≤ x.

◆ Greatest integer rule → [x] = n ⇔ n ≤ x < n + 1.

◆ Composition → (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)).

◆ Identity function → I(x) = x.

◆ Inverse function → f⁻¹, when the inverse relation is a function.

◆ Inverse procedure → interchange x and y, then solve for y.

◆ Inverse composition → f⁻¹ ∘ f = I and f ∘ f⁻¹ = I.

◆ Graph of inverse → reflection in y = x.

◆ Application model → identify variables, relation, domain and range before solving.
